# In Praise of the Dark

Somewhere within a few miles of you, almost certainly, there is a place where you could not see your own hand in front of your face. Not figuratively—literally. A closet, a cellar, a stretch of deep woods on a moonless night. True darkness has become one of the rarest experiences available to a human being, rarer than wilderness, rarer than silence. We live inside a permanent, glowing afternoon. By some estimates, four out of five North Americans have never seen the Milky Way with their naked eyes—not because it isn't there, hanging above the parking lots and cul-de-sacs, but because our own light drowns it out. We have built a civilization that treats darkness as a problem to be solved, and we have mostly solved it. The question worth asking is what, exactly, we solved away.

For nearly all of human history, nightfall was an event. It reorganized the world completely. When the sun went down, the rules changed: roads emptied, doors were barred, work stopped whether or not it was finished. Darkness was not merely inconvenient; it was genuinely dangerous, a time when the ordinary landscape turned hostile and unfamiliar. Every culture surrounded the night with its own apparatus of protection—prayers, charms, watchmen, superstitions. The English word *curfew* comes from the Old French *cuevrefeu*: "cover fire." It was a literal instruction, a bell rung in medieval towns telling households to bank their hearths and douse their candles, because an unattended flame in a city of timber was a catastrophe waiting for its moment. Night demanded management. It had to be survived, guarded against, waited out.

And yet—and this is the part our floodlit present has almost erased—the pre-industrial night was not only a threat. It had its own texture, its own economy, even its own pleasures. The historian Roger Ekirch, combing through diaries, letters, court records, and medical texts from the centuries before electric light, uncovered something startling: for most of Western history, people did not sleep through the night the way we do. They slept in two segments. There was the "first sleep," which began a couple of hours after dusk, and then, sometime past midnight, people simply woke up—for an hour, sometimes two—and then returned to the "second sleep" until dawn. This wasn't insomnia. It was the normal architecture of rest, mentioned so casually in old documents that no one thought to explain it. Doctors wrote about it. Prayer books assumed it. Travelers described it.

What did people do with that stolen hour in the middle of the night? Everything and nothing. They prayed—they believed the interval was especially suited to contemplation, the soul unarmored by daylight busyness. They talked. Husbands and wives, according to one old physician, were best advised to conceive children during these hours, when both body and spirit were rested and relaxed. Some got up and tended the fire, mended tools, read by rushlight, or stepped outside to check the weather by the stars. Neighbors visited neighbors. In villages, the midnight interval was a kind of unofficial social hour, quiet and intimate, lit by embers and moonlight. Then everyone lay back down and sank into the second sleep, waking with the sun. The night, in other words, once had rooms in it. We have since knocked them all together into a single long corridor of unconsciousness, and we pass through it without ever standing still.

Light itself was precious in that older world, and its price shaped behavior in ways we've forgotten. A beeswax candle was a luxury item; tallow candles, made from animal fat, were cheaper but smoked, sputtered, and smelled like a kitchen accident. The poorest households burned rushlights—dried rushes dipped in grease—which gave off a feeble glow and lasted barely an hour. Artificial light was measured out like medicine. Families gathered near the single source of it, which meant they gathered near each other, and the evening became communal by necessity: stories told aloud, songs sung, work done by shared illumination. Even travel bent around the moon. Armies scheduled marches to take advantage of moonlit nights; lovers' meetings and smugglers' runs alike were timed to the lunar calendar. The moon wasn't romantic decoration. It was infrastructure.

Then, in 1807, someone lit a row of gas lamps along London's Pall Mall, and the long retreat of the night began. Gaslight spread through the cities of Europe and America over the following decades, turning streets into corridors of yellow-orange glow. By the end of the nineteenth century, electric light arrived, and the transformation accelerated beyond anything the gaslight era could have imagined. Night became optional. Factories discovered they could run around the clock; cities discovered they could stay awake indefinitely. The twentieth century finished the job. Today the planet's surface glows so brightly from orbit that astronauts describe continents outlined in gold, and the night side of Earth looks less like darkness than like a circuit board left switched on.

We gained enormously—safety, productivity, medicine performed at 3 a.m., the simple freedom to read when we please. But something was traded away so gradually that no one signed for it, and the losses are only now coming into focus.

Consider what the light does to the body. Deep in the brain sits a cluster of cells called the suprachiasmatic nucleus, the master clock that keeps our physiology synchronized to the rotation of the planet. It takes its primary cue from light—specifically, from the blue-rich wavelengths that dominate daylight and, conveniently for device manufacturers, also dominate the emissions of our screens. When those wavelengths hit the retina in the evening, the clock receives a message it evolved over millions of years to obey: *it is daytime; stand down.* The pineal gland suppresses melatonin, the hormone that gathers sleepiness like a tide. We are, in effect, carrying portable noon into our bedrooms, and then wondering why the tide won't come in. The consequences ripple outward—fragmented sleep, grogginess, and, researchers increasingly suspect, contributions to longer-term troubles ranging from metabolic disorders to mood disorders. Shift workers, who live permanently at war with their own clocks, carry the heaviest burden; international health bodies have flagged severe circadian disruption as a probable carcinogen. None of this means light is poison. It means light is powerful, and power deserves respect.

The damage extends far past our own species, and arguably the animals have fared worse, since at least we chose this. Sea turtle hatchlings, emerging from their nests on beaches that their lineage has used for a hundred million years, instinctively crawl toward the brighter horizon—the open sea reflecting starlight. On developed coastlines, that ancient instruction now leads them toward beachfront hotels, parking lots, and highways, where they die by the thousands. Migrating birds, navigating at night by stars and magnetic fields, are drawn into the glare of cities; conservation groups in Chicago and elsewhere run "Lights Out" campaigns during migration season, asking buildings to dim, because the toll of collisions runs into the hundreds of millions of birds a year in North America alone. Insects spiral to their deaths around porch lights—one long-standing theory holds that moths steer by keeping a fixed angle to the moon, a perfectly sound strategy for a distant celestial body and a fatal one when the "moon" is forty watts and eighteen inches away. Even fireflies, those poets of the summer dusk, depend on darkness to speak: their entire courtship is a language of light, and in a glow-flooded suburb, nobody can hear anybody.

Perhaps my favorite illustration of what we've lost comes from Los Angeles, January 1994. An earthquake—the Northridge quake—knocked out power across huge swaths of the city in the middle of the night. And in the darkness, residents looked up and saw something vast and silvery and utterly alien stretched across the sky. Some of them, apparently having never seen it before, grew alarmed. Griffith Observatory reportedly received phone calls asking about the strange glowing cloud. Was it the earthquake? Was it dangerous? It was the Milky Way. Our own galaxy, visible from our own streets for the first time in generations, and it registered not as beauty but as anomaly—as something that didn't belong. That, to me, is one of the saddest and strangest sentences in modern history: people calling the authorities to report the universe.

Because here is the thing about the night sky: it is not a ceiling. It is a depth. The stars you see on a clear dark night are not points on a dome but objects scattered through distances so immense that light itself gets tired crossing them. Look at the Andromeda Galaxy—that faint oval smudge above the constellation Cassiopeia, visible to the naked eye from truly dark places—and you are seeing light that left home two and a half million years ago, before any member of our species existed. Every photon striking your retina is a fossil. The night sky is the deepest archive we possess, a record written in the only ink that survives such distances, and it plays nightly, free of charge, everywhere on Earth—except wherever we have accidentally censored it with our own glow.

There is also something the darkness does to the mind that brightness cannot. Stand under a genuinely dark sky and the first sensation is often vertigo—a sudden, recalibrating sense of scale, the ego quietly informed of its dimensions. Astronauts call the equivalent experience the overview effect, that cognitive shift that comes from seeing Earth whole. The dark sky offers a vertical version of it. But night also works on a smaller, more intimate register. Deprived of the visual field, the mind turns inward; this is why conversations change after dark, why confessions tend to happen at midnight, why grief and longing feel sharper at 2 a.m. than at 2 p.m. The night strips away the surfaces of things and leaves essence. Writers have always known this. Van Gogh painted *The Starry Night* from his window at the asylum in Saint-Rémy, working partly from memory and imagination, insisting that the night was more alive and more richly colored than the day. Keats addressed a star directly and envied it its steadfastness. And anyone who has watched a stubborn problem suddenly loosen at three in the morning—or woken with a sentence, a melody, a solution already assembled—knows that the sleeping mind keeps different office hours than the waking one, and files its best reports in the dark.

None of this argues for abolishing light, obviously. Nobody wants to return to tallow smoke and highway robbery. But there is a growing movement—astronomers, ecologists, insomniacs, romantics—arguing that we can have light without drowning in it, the way we learned we could have food without wasting half of it. The city of Flagstaff, Arizona, home to major observatories, became in 2001 the first officially designated International Dark Sky City, proving that a functioning municipality can light its streets with shielded, warm-toned, downward-facing fixtures and still see the galaxy from downtown. The principles are almost embarrassingly simple: light what needs lighting, when it needs lighting, pointing where it's needed. Use warmer colors. Turn things off. Much of our light pollution is not illumination but spillage—glare thrown sideways and upward, doing nothing for anyone except the moths and the satellites. The fix isn't sacrifice. It's intention.

So consider this an invitation. Some clear night near the next new moon, go somewhere darker than your living room—a park, a field, a roadside far from town—and give your eyes a real chance. Twenty minutes, minimum; the chemical adaptation of the retina is slow, and most people quit while their eyes are still mid-negotiation. Then look up. If you're lucky and patient, the faint river of the Milky Way will emerge, the way images develop in a tray, and you will be standing inside the oldest show on Earth, one that played for your ancestors every night of their lives, that played for the turtles and the moths and the migrating birds, that will still be playing long after the last screen goes dark.

We spent ten thousand years pushing back the night, and it was a magnificent achievement. But somewhere in the push, we mistook darkness for an enemy rather than a neighbor—an essential half of the world's rhythm, the resting beat, the pause that gives the music meaning. The dark is not the absence of anything. It is the presence of everything we've forgotten how to see.
